Q: Should I keep learning C++ or switch to Rust? A:

I recently had one of my projects (RTIC + embassy-stm32) reviewed by a Rust-beginner coworker. And while he struggled with the syntax at first, he had this "aha, wtf" moment when he realized how the borrow checker allows compile time ownership of peripherals, dmas, pins and interrupts, guaranteeing that if it compiles, you configured your pins, interrupts, dmas and peripherals correctly. And it just works.

Q: How should I extract a CSV data from Java Mission Control? A:

there's no one-click "Export to CSV" button for most of the JMC analysis tables (Method Profiling, Threads, etc.), but there are a few solid ways to get the data out.

1. Table copy (works today, no scripting)

In most JMC table views (e.g. the Threads page, the Method Table in Method Profiling), you can:

Select rows (Ctrl+A for all)

Right-click → Copy (or Ctrl+C)

Paste into a text file or spreadsheet — it comes out tab-delimited, which you can save as .tsv and open in Excel/Sheets, or convert to CSV with tr '\t' ','

This works well for smaller tables but is painful for large stack-trace tables with thousands of rows.

Q: Create programming language wihtout using any other PL A:

I did some coding in binary back in high school, on my Apple II+ microcomputer. It used a 6502 processor. I know assembly was an option, but my school didn't have an assembler, so I used a reference card that showed me the two-digit hexadecimal codes for 6502 instructions, like this one: https://6502.org/tutorials/6502opcodes.html

I typed in hex numbers directly. After a couple of days of that, you get to know the codes pretty well. It was over 40 years ago, but I still remember hex 4C is for the absolute jump instruction, which is like a GOTO, to move program execution to another address in the file.

That's still a programming language, by some definition. You're constrained to the instruction set of the processor you're writing for. There are commands like reading and writing data values in registers, adding them together, branching, and so on. It's tedious, but eventually you can code any program.

All other programming languages either compile to binary to run, or else they're interpreted by another application which is ultimately compiled to run as binary.

To execute a program on any modern OS, you'd at least have to write the file in an executable file format the OS recognizes. For example on the Mac, this format is called Mach-O. On Linux and UNIX, it's ELF. On Windows, it's PE.

If you don't want to use any processor instructions or OS file format, I think you've ruled out using any modern computer as we know them.

In theory, you could build your own machine that qualifies as a stored-program computer. That makes it able to run different programs without the machine itself needing to be rewired. These machines map program instructions to operations specific to that machine, which is again like binary code. But it would be an instruction set you designed, without reference to any other machine's instruction set.

Q: Accessing elements of Python dictionary by index A:

As I noticed your description, you just know that your parser will give you a dictionary that its values are dictionary too like this:

sampleDict = {
    "key1": {"key10": "value10", "key11": "value11"},
    "key2": {"key20": "value20", "key21": "value21"}
    }

So you have to iterate over your parent dictionary. If you want to print out or access all first dictionary keys in sampleDict.values() list, you may use something like this:

for key, value in sampleDict.items():
    print value.keys()[0]

If you want to just access first key of the first item in sampleDict.values(), this may be useful:

print sampleDict.values()[0].keys()[0]

If you use the example you gave in the question, I mean:

sampleDict = {
    'Apple': {'American':'16', 'Mexican':10, 'Chinese':5},
    'Grapes':{'Arabian':'25','Indian':'20'}
    }

The output for the first code is:

American
Indian

And the output for the second code is:

American

Update:

Above code examples do not work for version 3 and above of Python, since from version 3, Python changed the type of output of methods keys and values from list to dict_values. Type dict_values is not accepting indexing, but it is iterable. So you need to change above codes as below:

First One:

for key, value in sampleDict.items():
    print(list(value.keys())[0])

Second One:

print(list(list(sampleDict.values())[0].keys())[0])

Q: Static Class in Java A:

The static class must be inside another class to work, and that's because the static keyword tells the variable, function, or class to be accessed without needing to create an outer class, Meaning that classes are like methods and variables if they were inside an outer class. Q: Arduino IDE is not showing any port macOS A:

Turns out the Arduino IDE (likely arduino-cli) still needs uses some Intel era binaries. IDE 2.3.10 on my M3 macbook didn't detect the Arduino initially, but after installing rosetta, it worked:

softwareupdate --install-rosetta

IDE itself was failing silently, but the arduino-cli showed the following error, which helped me debug the problem:

Error starting discovery: discovery builtin:serial-discovery process not started: fork/exec /Users/dgupta/Library/Arduino15/packages/builtin/tools/serial-discovery/1.4.3/serial-discovery: bad CPU type in executable

Q: Is it possible to develop an iOS-like operating system based on RISC-V? A:

I'm not sure I understand the question. RISC-V is an ISA. Anything can be implemented in any ISA, as long as it supports basic building blocks like being turing complete and supporting i/o. Also ISA doesn't have performance. Concrete hardware implementing given ISA has performance.
